questions.prompt: A Castlebridge Logistics developer already has a Python script that polls an inbox, calls a model, and writes results to a database. Per Lesson 1, what does moving that same logic into a Power Automate flow actually buy them, if the model-calling logic itself doesn't change?
options: Built-in run history, retry policies, and human-approval steps around the same underlying pipeline, without hand-building that reliability plumbing themselves
A faster model response time, since Power Automate calls models through a lower-latency API than a Python SDK
The ability to run the exact same Python code completely unmodified, just hosted on Microsoft's servers instead of a laptop
Elimination of the need for any error handling, since Power Automate flows never fail
questions.explain: Power Automate doesn't make the model call itself different — it's the same trade you make with any managed service: retry policies, run history, audit logs, and approval steps come built in, instead of you hand-rolling a scheduler, retry queue, and webhook server around your own script. None of that reliability infrastructure is AI-specific; it's just a sensible place to put the plumbing around an AI call.

questions.prompt: By default, a new action's Run After setting only fires when the action right before it is successful — which is why one failure normally halts an entire flow. Which single configuration below correctly turns an action into a dedicated error-handling path that runs only when the previous action failed?
options: Uncheck "is successful" and check only "has failed"
Leave "is successful" checked and also check "has failed"
Check only "is skipped"
Check only "has timed out"
Leave the default settings and add a Condition action after it that tests for an error code
Rename the action "Catch" in its Settings tab
questions.explain: Run After's checkboxes are OR'd together — an action runs if any checked condition is true. To make an action run exclusively as an error path, "is successful" has to be unchecked and "has failed" checked in its place, so the action only fires when the step before it didn't work — exactly the mechanism behind the Try/Catch Scope pattern.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps "is successful" checked alongside "has failed", which means the action now runs whenever either condition is true — on success OR on failure, essentially every time the previous action isn't skipped or timed out. That's not an error-only path; it runs almost regardless of outcome, which defeats the point of a dedicated Catch step.

questions.prompt: A flow needs a running total that increments once per item inside an Apply to each loop. Per Lesson 3's rule about Initialize variable, where must the Initialize variable action actually be placed?
options: At the top level of the flow, before the Apply to each loop begins — then use Increment variable inside the loop on each pass
Inside the Apply to each loop, as the very first action, so it resets with every item
Inside a Condition branch checked once at the start of the flow
It doesn't matter — Initialize variable behaves identically no matter where it's placed
questions.explain: A variable can only be initialized at the top level of a flow — never inside a Condition branch, a Scope, or an Apply to each loop. A counter that needs to change inside a loop has to be initialized before the loop starts, at the top level, and then changed inside the loop with Set or Increment instead.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the HTTP action, per Lesson 4.
options: The action's five configurable fields are Method, URI, Headers, Queries, and Body — the same things any HTTP client sets
Its `body` output comes back already parsed into a typed object, unlike a raw `requests.post()` response, which stays an opaque string
A response status code of 200 or 202 generally signals success, while a 4xx or 5xx means something needs handling
An API key almost always has to be hardcoded directly into the URI field, since the Headers section can't carry authentication values
For calling Microsoft's own services with a managed identity instead of a static key, the HTTP action has a dedicated Authentication section under advanced options
questions.explain: The HTTP action configures the same five things any HTTP client needs: Method, URI, Headers, Queries, and Body. Its `body` output lands as a single opaque string until something parses it — the opposite of option B. Status codes work the same as anywhere else: 200/202 signal success, 4xx/5xx need handling. An API key normally goes in Headers, not the URI, which is also where the dedicated Authentication section under advanced options lives for Microsoft's own services.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: instead of hand-writing a JSON schema for Parse JSON, you can run the flow once, copy a real example of the response body, and use the ________ feature to have Power Automate write the schema for you.
questions.explain: Generate from sample lets you paste in a real example payload and have Power Automate write the JSON schema for you — the same "generate from an example, not a hand-written spec" workflow familiar from tools like json-schema-generator, built directly into the designer.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building and test-running a brand-new flow, per Lesson 2, in the correct order.
items: Select the plus sign below the last step and choose an action from the Add an action pane
Select Save, which runs a validation pass and refuses to save if something is misconfigured
Select Test, then choose Manually to trigger one run by hand
Watch each action complete with a green checkmark, then check run history for the full input and output of each step
questions.explain: An action is added from the Add an action pane, then Save runs a validation pass before anything persists — the same way a compiler refuses to produce a binary from code with a syntax error. Only once a flow saves cleanly does Test become available, and a manual test run's full input and output at every step lands in run history, the first place to look when a flow doesn't behave as expected.

questions.prompt: Castlebridge wants an AI Builder model that reads its own specific delivery-confirmation PDF layout, a layout nobody outside the company has ever seen. Per Lesson 7, which kind of model is this, and what does building it require?
options: A custom model — Castlebridge must upload and tag at least five of its own sample documents before it can be trained
A prebuilt model — it's ready to use immediately with no training, the same as AI Builder's general sentiment analysis model
A custom model — but it trains itself automatically the first time it sees a real Castlebridge document in production, with no upload step
A prebuilt model — but only after Microsoft adds Castlebridge's specific layout to its training set on request
questions.explain: Prebuilt models are ready immediately because Microsoft already trained them on general data; custom models are trained on an organization's own data, with no one else's data teaching the model what a Castlebridge document looks like. Training is a guided wizard: upload samples, tag the fields or categories, and let AI Builder run the training job — which for a document processing model means at least five tagged sample documents.

questions.prompt: A Process documents action extracts a ShipmentID field from a delivery confirmation. Per Lesson 8, what two separate pieces of dynamic content does that one tagged field actually produce for later steps?
options: `ShipmentID value` (the extracted text) and `ShipmentID confidence score` (a 0-1 number showing how sure the model is)
Just `ShipmentID value` — confidence scores are only produced for table columns, not single fields
`ShipmentID value` and `ShipmentID page number` — the page of the document the field was found on
A single combined token containing both the value and the confidence score as one string
questions.explain: Every tagged field becomes two separate pieces of dynamic content: `<field> value`, the extracted text, number, or date, and `<field> confidence score`, a 0-1 number expressing how sure the model is. A high score like 0.97 is safe to trust automatically; a low score is a signal to route the document to a human instead.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AI Builder's classification and image models, per Lesson 9.
options: A custom category classification model is trained on a Dataverse table of sample text paired with the category each sample belongs to
The image description model sorts a photo into one of the categories you defined when training it, the same way text classification works
A classification model's output — a category label plus a confidence score — is usually followed by a Condition or Switch action that routes based on the label
Object detection is a custom model category you train on your own labeled images, for recognizing something more specific than a general image description
There's no prebuilt classification model available for text — every text classifier has to be custom-trained
questions.explain: Category classification trains on a Dataverse table pairing sample text with tags. Its output — a label plus confidence score — naturally feeds a Condition or Switch. Object detection is a custom category for recognizing specific objects in images. Image description, unlike category classification, doesn't sort into predefined categories at all — it generates a plain-language description and tags. And a prebuilt category classification model does exist, tuned for general customer feedback.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Run a prompt action was previously named ________ before May 2025.
acceptedAnswers: Create text with GPT using a prompt
questions.explain: Run a prompt is the current name for the action that executes an AI Builder prompt; older tutorials and existing flows built before May 2025 may still show it as Create text with GPT using a prompt, the same action under its previous name.

questions.prompt: A Castlebridge shipment-triage prompt's JSON output is left on Auto-detected while the team keeps iterating on the prompt's wording. Per Lesson 11, what's the actual risk of staying on Auto-detected once a downstream flow is built against specific key names like shipmentId?
options: The inferred JSON shape can change the next time the prompt is tested, silently breaking any action downstream that expects those specific key names
Auto-detected mode caps the response at a single key, so shipmentId, requestedDate, and urgent could never all appear together
Auto-detected format requires manually re-entering the schema by hand every time the prompt runs
There's no actual risk — Auto-detected and Custom behave identically once a flow is in production
questions.explain: Auto-detected infers the JSON shape fresh every time the prompt is tested — convenient while still iterating, but exactly the wrong choice once a flow downstream depends on specific key names. Custom format locks in a shape from a provided example so it never silently changes, even as the prompt's instructions keep getting tweaked.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 12's three-layer stack to what it actually is.
right: The Azure resource that actually hosts the GPT-family model AI Builder prompts call underneath
The specific Azure OpenAI REST API a direct HTTP action posts a list of messages to
The simplest layer — write instructions in prompt builder's own interface, with the connection to the model handled for you
The wider family Azure OpenAI belongs to, including services like Azure AI Language and Azure AI Document Intelligence
questions.explain: AI Builder prompts are the simplest layer, with prompt builder's interface handling the model connection for you. Azure OpenAI Service is the Azure resource actually hosting the GPT-family model underneath. Azure AI Services is the wider family Azure OpenAI belongs to, alongside services like Azure AI Language and Azure AI Document Intelligence. The chat completions endpoint is the specific Azure OpenAI REST API a direct HTTP action posts messages to.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of Lesson 13's end-to-end AI document processing flow in the order they actually run.
items: Trigger: When a new email arrives (V3), filtered to emails with attachments
Extract: Process documents pulls ShipmentID, InvoiceTotal, DueDate, and the Items table from the attachment
Branch on confidence: a Condition checks the ShipmentID confidence score and routes low-confidence extractions to a Teams channel for manual entry
Structure: a JSON-output Run a prompt action cross-checks the extracted total against the line items
Human review: a Condition on totalsMatch routes any mismatch into Start and wait for an approval of text
Record: Add a row into a table writes the final confirmed values to the accounting Excel Online table
questions.explain: The flow starts with the email trigger, extracts fields with Process documents, then branches on the extraction's own confidence score before trusting it. Only after that does a JSON-output prompt cross-check the total against line items, with a second Condition routing any mismatch to human approval. Whatever makes it through — automatically or after approval — gets recorded last, in the accounting table.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 14, what's the actual difference in design approach between building a Power Automate flow and building a Copilot Studio agent for the same support-ticket task?
options: A flow is deterministic — you draw the exact path from trigger to outcome; an agent is reasoning-driven — you give it instructions and tools, and it decides the path itself at runtime
There's no real difference — a Copilot Studio agent is just a Power Automate flow renamed and relicensed separately
A flow can call AI models, but an agent can only use pre-trained categories and can never generate new text
An agent always runs faster than a flow, because it skips the trigger-and-action model entirely
questions.explain: A Power Automate flow always takes the exact path you designed — that's what deterministic means here. A Copilot Studio agent is reasoning-driven: you give it instructions, knowledge, and tools, and at runtime it decides which to use and in what order, based on what was actually asked. That's a meaningfully different design job — writing a job description instead of drawing a flowchart.

questions.prompt: Lesson 15 has you test a brand-new agent with no tools or knowledge sources attached yet, before building anything else. What's the actual reason for testing this early, instead of waiting until the agent is fully built?
options: It establishes a baseline, so once tools and knowledge are layered on later, a weird response can be traced to a bad instruction, a missing knowledge source, or a misfiring tool — instead of all three being tangled together
Copilot Studio requires at least one successful test before any tool can be attached to an agent
It permanently locks the agent's instructions, preventing any further edits
It's the only way to generate the agent's icon and description
questions.explain: Testing an agent with nothing attached establishes what it does with just its instructions. Once tools, knowledge, and flows get layered on in later lessons, that baseline is what makes it possible to tell whether a weird response comes from a bad instruction, a missing knowledge source, or a misfiring tool, rather than guessing among all three at once.

questions.prompt: Which pair of requirements must a flow actually satisfy before Copilot Studio will even let you attach it to an agent as a tool?
options: The "When an agent calls the flow" trigger, plus a "Respond to the agent" action configured with its Asynchronous response toggle set to Off
The "When an agent calls the flow" trigger, plus a "Respond to the agent" action configured with its Asynchronous response toggle set to On
Any HTTP-triggered flow, plus a Terminate action with its status set to Succeeded
A Recurrence trigger that runs at least once per day, plus a Start and wait for an approval action
The "When an agent calls the flow" trigger by itself — no response action is required at all
A "Respond to the agent" action triggered by any connector, with no specific trigger type required
questions.explain: A flow becomes eligible to be attached as a tool only with the dedicated "When an agent calls the flow" trigger and a "Respond to the agent" action, and that action's Asynchronous response toggle has to be Off so the flow responds synchronously — the agent is waiting live on the other end of the call, within a 100-second limit, so an asynchronous response would never reach it in time.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B gets both required pieces right — the trigger and the response action — but flips the one setting that actually matters: turning Asynchronous response On means the flow doesn't hand its result back on the same synchronous call the waiting agent needs, which is exactly the opposite of what the flow has to do to qualify as a tool.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about generative orchestration, per Lesson 17.
options: Classic orchestration matches a user's message against trigger phrases you defined for each topic, and runs the single best-matching topic
Generative orchestration can chain more than one tool together, in sequence, for a single user request
Of the signals the orchestrator weighs when choosing a tool, the tool's description carries the most weight
A tool named "Get EPS" with the description "Gets EPS for any stock ticker" is a good example of a clear tool description, since EPS is unambiguous
Generative orchestration can only ever call zero or exactly one tool per user message, never more than one
questions.explain: Classic orchestration matches fixed trigger phrases to a single topic. Generative orchestration, by contrast, can chain more than one tool in sequence, and the description of each tool, topic, or knowledge source carries the most weight in how the orchestrator chooses. The "Get EPS" example is specifically called out as a bad description because it leans on jargon instead of plain language — and generative orchestration is not capped at one tool per message; that's exactly what chaining means.

questions.prompt: Match each Lesson 18 approval action or approval type to what it actually controls.
left: Start and wait for an approval
right: Creates the approval request but doesn't wait, meant to be paired with a separate Wait for an approval action elsewhere so other work can happen in parallel
Creates the request and pauses the flow at that step until a response comes back — the usual choice for a human-in-the-loop gate
Approvers respond one at a time, in a defined order; each must respond before the next is asked
Any one assigned approver's response completes the request
questions.explain: Start and wait for an approval creates the request and pauses the flow until a response arrives — the usual choice for a human-in-the-loop gate. Create an approval creates the request without waiting, meant to pair with a separate Wait for an approval action so other work can run in parallel. Among approval types, First to respond completes as soon as any one assigned approver answers, while Sequential approval requires approvers to respond one at a time, in a defined order.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: rules configured in the Power Platform admin center that govern which connectors and capabilities agents in an environment are allowed to use at all are called ________ policies.
questions.explain: Data loss prevention (DLP) policies are configured in the Power Platform admin center and govern which connectors and capabilities agents in a given environment are allowed to use — how an organization prevents an agent from being built with, say, a connector to an unapproved external service.

questions.prompt: Put these events of the capstone's Castlebridge Support Triage Agent system in the order they actually happen for a ticket that ends up needing escalation.
items: A new ticket lands in the support inbox, and the Castlebridge Support Triage Agent reads it
The agent calls the Classify Support Ticket tool, which returns a category, urgency, and a proposedAction
Because proposedAction is "escalate", a second, separately triggered flow runs Start and wait for an approval with the First to respond type
A support lead responds to the approval request
Only after that approval comes back does the second flow actually notify the escalation contact
questions.explain: The agent reads the ticket and calls its classification tool, which returns a structured result including proposedAction. Because the synchronous tool flow never performs the escalation itself, a separate flow — triggered independently — runs the approval step with no 100-second constraint, and only once a support lead actually responds does that second flow notify the escalation contact. Nothing auto-escalates without a person agreeing first.
